claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase microstructure consisting of an FCC matrix and intermetallic or σ-phase regions.
The dual-phase microstructure can have a refined eutectic or hypereutectic morphology.
Oxide films can form on HEAs during elevated-temperature exposure or friction and wear.
The oxide film on the target multiphase eutectic alloy is unevenly protective.
The constituent phases have different oxidation kinetics and electrochemical properties.
Electrochemical-potential differences between the phases generate localized galvanic cells.
Differential oxidation of the phases produces a heterogeneous passive or oxide film.
Mechanical wear continually removes or damages the heterogeneous oxide film and exposes fresh alloy surfaces.
Freshly exposed surfaces corrode more rapidly because of micro-galvanic interactions between the phases.
Repeated oxide-film formation and mechanical removal amplifies both wear and corrosion beyond their isolated effects.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will produce total degradation greater than the sum of the isolated wear and corrosion effects.
Under simultaneous exposure, the alloy will have a higher wear rate than the matched wear-only baseline.
Under simultaneous exposure, the alloy will have a higher corrosion current density than the matched corrosion-only baseline.
Elevated temperature promotes active oxide-film formation or reformation.
Aggressive chloride ions and wear sufficient to disrupt passivity are necessary boundary conditions for the proposed acceleration.
The quantitative magnitude of the acceleration depends on phase distribution, oxide-film properties, and test conditions.
